en: Dīgha Nikāya 23:
The Discourse to Pāyāsi Thus have I heard.

On one occasion, while the Venerable Kumārakassapa was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus numbering about five hundred, he arrived at a city of the Kosalans named Setavyā.
There, the Venerable Kumārakassapa stayed to the north of Setavyā in the Siṁsapā Grove.

Now at that time, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi was residing in Setavyā—a place teeming with living beings, abundant in grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal domain granted as a royal gift and a brahminical endowment by King Pasenadi of Kosala. At that time, a pernicious view such as this had arisen in the royal chaplain Pāyāsi: [The rest of the passage follows: "Only these two things are true, all else is false: giving, sacrifice, and offering do not exist; there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds; this world and the other world do not exist; there is no mother or father; and there are no spontaneously born beings; in this world there are no recluses or brahmins who have attained right conduct and right practice, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known to others. [The passage continues with the account of his debate with Venerable Kumāra Kassapa. [The passage concludes with: Then the royal chaplain Pāyāsi, having spoken thus, rose from his seat and departed. Then, some time later, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi fell ill; he was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. He summoned a certain man and said to him: "Come, my good man, go to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa and, having approached him, pay homage in my name with your head at his feet, and say: 'Venerable sir, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi is ill, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; he pays homage with his head at the Venerable One's feet. And say: 'Venerable sir, may the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa come to the residence of the royal chaplain Pāyāsi out of compassion. "Yes, sir," that man replied to the royal chaplain Pāyāsi. He went to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, and having approached him, he paid homage with his head at his feet and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa: "Venerable sir, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi pays homage with his head at the Venerable One's feet and says: 'Venerable sir, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi is ill, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; he pays homage with his head at the Venerable One's feet. And he says: 'Venerable sir, may the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa come to the residence of the royal chaplain Pāyāsi out of compassion. "Very well, friend," the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa replied to that man. Then the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of the royal chaplain Pāyāsi with a companion bhikkhu. On arrival, he sat down on the prepared seat. The royal chaplain Pāyāsi then approached the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, paid homage with his head at his feet, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said to him: "Is it true, Pāyāsi, that a pernicious view such as this has arisen in you: 'Only these two things are true, all else is false: giving, sacrifice, and offering do not exist... there are no spontaneously born beings; in this world there are no recluses or brahmins who have attained right conduct and right practice... [The dialogue between Pāyāsi and Kumāra Kassapa continues, with Pāyāsi presenting his arguments and Kassapa providing refutations based on logic, scripture, and common experience. [The passage concludes with: When this was said, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi said to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa: "Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa in many ways. I go to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. From this day forth, may the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. "But, Pāyāsi, you have many supporters and attendants who hold views different from yours. It is possible that they, when you are gone, will cause trouble for you. Come, Pāyāsi, let us go to them. "Yes, venerable sir," the royal chaplain Pāyāsi replied to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa. Then the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, together with the royal chaplain Pāyāsi, went to the royal chaplain Pāyāsi’s supporters and attendants. On arrival, he sat down on the prepared seat. The royal chaplain Pāyāsi then approached those people, paid homage with his head at their feet, and stood to one side. As he was standing there, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said to them: "Is it true, sirs, that a pernicious view such as this has arisen in your master: 'Only these two things are true, all else is false: giving, sacrifice, and offering do not exist... there are no spontaneously born beings; in this world there are no recluses or brahmins who have attained right conduct and right practice... [The dialogue continues, with the supporters and attendants expressing their agreement with Pāyāsi's views. [The passage concludes with: When this was said, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi said to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa: "Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned... even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa in many ways. I go to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. From this day forth, may the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa accept me and these people as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life. "But, Pāyāsi, you have many enemies and adversaries who hold views different from yours. It is possible that they, when you are gone, will cause trouble for you. Come, Pāyāsi, let us go to them. "Yes, venerable sir," the royal chaplain Pāyāsi replied to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa. Then the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, together with the royal chaplain Pāyāsi, went to the royal chaplain Pāyāsi’s enemies and adversaries. On arrival, he sat down on the prepared seat. The royal chaplain Pāyāsi then approached those people, paid homage with his head at their feet, and stood to one side. As he was standing there, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said to them: "Is it true, sirs, that a pernicious view such as this has arisen in your master: 'Only these two things are true, all else is false: giving, sacrifice, and offering do not exist... there are no spontaneously born beings; in this world there are no recluses or brahmins who have attained right conduct and right practice... [The dialogue continues, with the enemies and adversaries expressing their agreement with Pāyāsi's views. [The passage concludes with: When this was said, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi said to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa: "Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned... even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa in many ways. I go to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. From this day forth, may the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa accept me and these people as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life. "But, Pāyāsi, you have many friends and colleagues who hold views different from yours. It is possible that they, when you are gone, will cause trouble for you. Come, Pāyāsi, let us go to them. "Yes, venerable sir," the royal chaplain Pāyāsi replied to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa. Then the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, together with the royal chaplain Pāyāsi, went to the royal chaplain Pāyāsi’s friends and colleagues. On arrival, he sat down on the prepared seat. The royal chaplain Pāyāsi then approached those people, paid homage with his head at their feet, and stood to one side. As he was standing there, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said to them:
“Thus: ‘There is no other world; there are no beings of spontaneous birth; there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds.
Now the brahmin householders of Setavyā heard:
‘The ascetic Kumāra Kassapa, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, has arrived [here].’”
Accompanied by a great community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks,
he arrived at Setavyā and was staying to the north of Setavyā in the Siṃsapā Grove.
Now, this excellent report concerning the venerable Kumāra Kassapa had spread abroad:
“He is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, eloquent, and possessed of ready wit; he is both aged and an arahant.
It is indeed good to see such arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Setavyā, departing from Setavyā in groups and bands, went northward toward the Siṃsapā Grove.
Now at that time, the royal counselor Pāyāsi had gone up to the upper palace for his midday rest.
The royal counselor Pāyāsi saw the brahmin householders of Setavyā leaving Setavyā in groups and crowds, heading north toward the Siṃsapā Grove;
seeing them, he addressed his steward:
“Sir, minister, why is it that the brahmin householders of Setavyā have departed from Setavyā in groups and crowds, heading north toward the Siṃsapā Grove?
“There is, sir, a recluse named Kumāra Kassapa, a disciple of the recluse Gotama.
While wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, he has arrived at Setavyā.”
He is staying north of Setavyā in the Siṃsapā Grove.
Now, this good report has spread concerning the venerable Kumāra Kassapa:
“He is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, an eloquent speaker, possessed of ready wit, and both aged and an arahant.”
“Therefore, we are approaching the venerable Kumāra Kassapa for an audience.
“In that case, my good charioteer, go to where the brahmin householders of Setavyā are; having approached them, speak thus to the brahmin householders of Setavyā:
‘The royal prince Pāyāsi says this:’”
"Let your honors wait; Prince Pāyāsi will also approach to see the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa.

Before the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa convinces the foolish and incompetent brahmin householders of Setavyā that 'there is indeed another world, there are beings of spontaneous birth, and there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done.'"
“There is no other world, Master Steward; there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there is no fruit or result of good or evil deeds.
“Yes, sir,” the steward replied to Pāyāsi the prince, and he went to the brahmin householders of Setavyā. Having approached them, he said to the brahmin householders of Setavyā:
“Gentlemen, Prince Pāyāsi says this: ‘May you wait, gentlemen, for Prince Pāyāsi will also go to see the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa.’”
Then the royal prince Pāyāsi, surrounded by the brahmin householders of Setavyā, approached the Siṃsapā Grove where the Venerable Kumārakassapa was staying.
Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Kumārakassapa;
after exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Some of the brahmin householders of Setavyā paid homage to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa and sat down to one side;
some exchanged greetings with the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa,
and having concluded those polite and courteous words of greeting, they sat down to one side.
Some, having extended their joined palms toward the Venerable Kumārakassapa, sat down to one side.
Some, having announced their name and clan, sat down to one side.
Some, remaining silent, sat down to one side.
2. The Doctrine of Nihilism Seated to one side, the royal prince Pāyāsi said this to the Venerable Kumārakassapa:
“Master Kassapa, I am of such a doctrine and such a view:”
‘Thus there is no other world, there are no beings who arise spontaneously, and there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.
“Prince, I have neither seen nor heard of anyone who speaks and holds such a view.
How indeed could one say: [...]"?
‘Is it thus that there is no other world, no beings who arise spontaneously, and no fruit or result of good and evil deeds?
‘In that case, Prince, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit. 2.1. The Simile of the Sun and Moon:
‘In that case, Prince, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.’
“What do you think, royal sage, are these sun and moon in this world or in another world? Are they gods or humans?
“Venerable Kassapa, these sun and moon are in another world, not in this one; they are gods, not humans.”
“By this method also, Prince, let it be so for you:
‘Indeed, there is another world; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done.
“Even though Master Kassapa says this, nevertheless, this is how it appears to me in this matter:”
‘Thus there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds.
‘But, royal sage, is there a method by which it occurs to you that:
“Thus there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds”?’
“There is, Master Kassapa, a way in which it occurs to me thus: ‘In this way, there is no other world;
there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.
“In what way, Prince?”

“Here, Master Kassapa, my friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives are killers of living beings, takers of what is not given, sexual misconducters, speakers of falsehood, slanders, harsh speech, and idle chatter; they are covetous, ill-willed, and hold wrong views.
At a later time, they become afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
When I know this:”
‘They will not recover from this affliction,’ thinking thus, I would approach them and say:
‘Sirs, there are certain recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Those who take life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, speak maliciously, speak harshly, and indulge in idle chatter...’”’
“Covetous, with minds of ill will, and holding wrong views, they—upon the breakup of the body, after death—reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

Sirs, you are indeed those who take life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, speak divisively, speak harshly, and indulge in idle chatter; you are covetous, with minds of ill will, and hold wrong views.

If the word of those venerable recluses and brahmins is true, then upon the breakup of the body, after death, you will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But if, sirs, upon the breakup of the body, after death, you should be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell, then come to me and report:
"In this way, there is another world; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done."
"Sirs, you are indeed trustworthy and reliable; what you have seen will be exactly as if you had seen it yourselves.
Having agreed to this by saying "Very well," they neither came back to inform me nor did they send a messenger.
This, Master Kassapa, is the way in which I come to this conclusion: [that the Tathāgata does not exist after death].
‘Thus there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds.
“In that case, royal sage, I shall question you on this very matter. Answer as you see fit.”
"What do you think, royal sage?
Suppose some men here were to seize a thief caught in the act of wrongdoing and bring him before you, saying:
'Venerable sir, this is a thief caught in the act of wrongdoing;'"
‘Whatever punishment you wish for him, inflict it.
You should say to them:
‘In that case, sirs, bind this man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope and bind him.’”
“Having shaved his head, lead him with a harsh-sounding drum from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads,
then exit through the southern gate and cut off his head at the execution ground to the south of the city.
Having replied, “Very well,” they bound that man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope.
Having shaved his head and led him around from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads with a harsh-sounding drum,
they would lead him out through the southern gate and have him seated at the place of execution to the south of the city.
Would that thief then receive [any recognition] from the executioners?

‘Wait, sirs, executioners, until I have designated my friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen in such-and-such a village or town, and then I shall return’—would the executioners cut off the head of one who was merely prattling on like this?
“Certainly not, Master Kassapa; that thief would not obtain [such a reprieve] from the executioners.”
“‘Let the executioners wait, sirs, until I have visited my friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations in such-and-such a village or town, so that I may return after having informed them.
Yet the executioners would cut off his head while he was still thus prattling.
“Indeed, O royal sage, that thief—a mere human being—would find no protection among his fellow humans who are the executioners.”
‘Wait, sirs, executioners, until I have designated my friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives in such-and-such a village or town, and then I shall return.

But what of those friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives—were they not themselves killers of living beings, takers of what is not given, indulgers in sexual misconduct, speakers of falsehood, slanders, harsh speech, and idle chatter;
were they not covetous, ill-willed, and holders of wrong views? [What of them] when their bodies...
After passing away, having been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, and hell, will they obtain this from the guardians of hell:
"Wait a moment, sirs, guardians of hell, until we go and inform King Pāyāsi:
'Thus indeed there is another world; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there is the fruit and result of well-done and ill-done deeds'?"
“By this method also, Prince, let it be so for you:
‘Thus indeed there is another world; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there is fruit and result of deeds well-done and ill-done.
“Even though Master Kassapa speaks thus, nevertheless, in this matter, this is my view:”
‘Thus there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds.
‘But, royal sage, is there some method by which you hold such a view as this:
“Thus there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds”?’
“There is, Master Kassapa, a way in which it occurs to me thus: ‘In this way, there is no other world;
there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds.
“In what way, Prince?”
“Here, Master Kassapa, my friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations abstain from the destruction of life,
abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from malicious speech,
abstain from harsh speech, and abstain from idle chatter; they are free from covetousness, free from ill will, and possess right view.”
At a later time, they became afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
When I knew,
"They will not now recover from this illness," I approached them and spoke thus:
“Indeed, sir, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘Those who abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct,
abstain from false speech, abstain from malicious speech, abstain from harsh speech, and abstain from idle chatter...’”
“Being free from covetousness, with minds free from ill will, and possessing right view, they— upon the breakup of the body, after death—
reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Now, sirs, you are abstainers from taking life, abstainers from taking what is not given, and abstainers from sexual misconduct.
They abstain from false speech, abstain from malicious speech, abstain from harsh speech, and abstain from idle chatter;
they are free from covetousness, free from ill will, and possess right view.
If the word of those venerable recluses and brahmins is true, then upon the breakup of the body, after death, you will be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“If, sirs, after the breakup of the body, after death, you should be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, please come to me and report:
‘Indeed, there is another world; there are beings who are spontaneously born; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done.
For you are trustworthy and reliable to me; what you have seen will be exactly as if you had seen it yourself.”
Having agreed to me, saying "That is not right," they neither came back to inform me nor did they send a messenger.
This, Master Kassapa, is the way in which it occurs to me:
"Thus, there is no other world; there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds."

2.3. The Simile of the Manure Pit “Therefore, royal sage, I shall give you a simile. For by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said. Suppose, royal sage, there were a man who was poor, needy, and destitute, and he had fallen into debt to others. He would be pursued by creditors, and being harassed by them, he would flee to the forest. There, while wandering through the forest, he would come upon a large pit filled with excrement, deep and full to the brim. To escape his pursuers, he would leap into that pit of excrement. Having leaped in, he would sink down into it up to his neck. Then, two strong men would seize both his arms and pull him out. Once pulled out, they would wash off the excrement from his body with warm water until he was clean and free of filth. Then, having dressed him in clean clothes and anointed him with fragrant sandalwood oil, they would place him in a carriage drawn by thoroughbred horses and lead him to the king’s palace. Seated there on a high, luxurious couch, he would enjoy the finest delicacies of various flavors. What do you think, royal sage? Would that man, having experienced such great wealth and honor, remember his former state of poverty, need, and destitution? “Certainly, venerable sir; he would remember it. “But, royal sage, that man would not even think, ‘I have been so poor, needy, and destitute,’ let alone remember the specific details. Why is that? Because he has now attained such great wealth and honor. In the same way, royal sage, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he does not even think, ‘I am subject to birth,’ let alone remember the specific details of his former state. What are these four? Here, royal sage, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way;

that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and leading to concentration. Possessing these four qualities, royal sage, a noble disciple does not even think, ‘I am subject to birth,’ let alone remember the specific details of his former state of poverty, need, and destitution. Why is that? Because he has now attained such great wealth and honor.”’”
Suppose, royal prince, a man were submerged head-first in a pit of excrement.
You would then command your men:
"Come now, sirs, pull that man out of that pit of excrement."
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” they would pull that man out of that cesspit.
You should then say to them:
“In that case, sirs, wipe the excrement thoroughly from that man’s body with bamboo scrapers.”
Having agreed, saying "Very well," they would thoroughly scrub the excrement from that man's body with bamboo scrapers.
You should then say to them:
"In that case, sirs, rub that man's body three times with yellow clay until it is well-polished."
Suppose they were to rub that man’s body three times with yellow clay.
You might say to them:
“In that case, sirs, anoint that man with oil and wash him thoroughly three times with fine powder.”
Having anointed that man with oil and washed him thoroughly three times with fine powder,
they would say to you:
“In that case, sir, have this man’s hair and beard trimmed.”
Suppose they were to shave off that man’s hair and beard.
You would then say to them:
“In that case, sirs, bring for that man costly garlands, costly ointments, and costly garments.”
They would bring that man costly garlands, costly ointments, and costly clothes.
You would then say to them:
“In that case, sirs, having led that man up to the palace, provide him with the five strands of sensual pleasure.”
Having led that man up to the palace, they would provide him with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
What do you think, royal sage,
regarding that man who is well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard well-trimmed, and adorned with garlands and ornaments?

“Would there be a desire in one who is dressed in white garments, having gone to the top of a magnificent palace, endowed with and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure while being entertained,
to plunge once again into that pit of excrement?
“Certainly not, Master Kassapa.”
“And for what reason?

“Because, Master Kassapa, that cesspool of excrement is impure and reckoned as impure, foul-smelling and reckoned as foul-smelling, disgusting and reckoned as disgusting, and repulsive and reckoned as repulsive.

“In the same way, royal prince, humans are impure to the gods and reckoned as impure; they are foul-smelling and reckoned as foul-smelling; they are disgusting and reckoned as disgusting; and they are repulsive and reckoned as repulsive.”
"O royal prince, the human scent extends for a hundred yojanas and overpowers the gods.
Now, did those friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives of yours abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given,
abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from malicious and harsh speech?"

Abstaining from idle chatter, free from covetousness, with minds devoid of ill will, and possessing right view, they—upon the breakup of the body, after death—will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Having come back, will they report:
‘Thus indeed there is another world; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done’?”
“By this method, too, O royal sage, let it be so for you:
‘Thus indeed there is another world; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done.
“Even though Master Kassapa speaks thus, nevertheless, this is how it appears to me in this matter:”
‘Thus: there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds.
‘But, royal sage, is there a method by which...?
‘There is, Master Kassapa, a method by which...’
"In what way, O Kṣatriya?

‘In this case, Master Kassapa, my friends, colleagues, kinsmen, and blood relatives abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from the use of intoxicants, liquor, and spirits which cause heedlessness.
At a later time, they become afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.’”
When I know:
"These people will not recover from this illness," I approach them and say:
"Sirs, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view: [that one experiences the results of deeds in this very life]."
“Those who abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech,
and abstain from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence— upon the breakup of the body, after death,
they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.”

Sirs, you indeed abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.

If the word of those venerable recluses and brahmins is true, then upon the dissolution of the body, after death, you will be reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
“If, sir, after the breakup of the body, after death, you should be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, please come to me and report:
‘Thus indeed there is another world; there are beings who are spontaneously born; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done.
For you are trustworthy and reliable to me; whatever you have seen, this will be exactly as if you had seen it yourself.”
Having agreed to me, saying “That is not good,” they neither come back to inform me nor do they send a messenger.
This, Master Kassapa, is the way in which it occurs to me:
“Thus indeed there is no other world, there are no beings who arise spontaneously, and there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.”
2.4. The Simile of the Tāvatiṃsa Devas “In that case, royal sage, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.

2.10. The Simile of the Fire-Worshipping Ascetic “In that case, royal sage, I shall give you a simile.

Once upon a time, royal sage, a certain fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic was dwelling in a leaf-hut in a forest tract.
Then, royal sage, a certain caravan set out from a certain district.
That caravan stayed for one night near the hermitage of that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic and then departed.
Then, royal sage, it occurred to that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic:
"What if I were to go to where that caravan encampment is? Perhaps I might find some useful article there.

Then, rising early in the morning, that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic went to where that caravan encampment was. Having arrived, he saw in that caravan encampment a young boy, weak and lying on his back, abandoned there.
Having seen this, it occurred to him:
"It would not be fitting for me that a human being should pass away while I am looking on.
Suppose I were to take this boy to my hermitage, raise him, nourish him, and bring him up."
Then that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic, having led the boy to his hermitage, raised him, nourished him, and brought him up.
When the boy was ten years old or twelve years old, a certain business arose for that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic in the countryside.
Then that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic said this to the boy:
‘Father, I wish to go to the countryside;
you, father, should tend the fire.
And let not the fire go out.’
‘And if your fire should go out, here is an axe, here is wood, and here is a fire-drill; having produced fire, you should tend the fire.
Then that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic, having thus instructed the boy, went away to the countryside.
While he was absorbed in his play, the fire went out.
Then this thought occurred to that boy:
"My father said this to me:
'My dear son, you should tend the fire.'"
“Let not your fire go out.
And if your fire should go out, here is an adze, here is wood, and here is a fire-drill; having kindled a fire, you should tend the fire. [He thought:
“What if I were to kindle a fire and tend the fire?”
Then that boy split a bundle of fire-sticks with an axe,
thinking, "Perhaps I might obtain fire.
But he did not obtain fire.
He split the fire-sticks in two, he split them into three, he split them into four, he split them into five, he split them into ten, he split them into a hundred;
he reduced them to pieces, and having reduced them to pieces, he pounded them in a mortar;
having pounded them in the mortar, he winnowed them in a strong wind.
‘Perhaps I might obtain fire.
But he did not obtain fire.
Then that fire-worshipper, the matted-hair ascetic, having completed his business in the countryside, approached his own hermitage; having approached, he said this to the boy:
‘I hope, dear son, that the fire has not gone out?
‘Just now, father, while I was absorbed in play, the fire went out.
Then this thought occurred to me:’
“My father said this to me: ‘My son, you should tend the fire.
And let not the fire go out on you, my son.
But if the fire should go out on you, here is an axe, here is firewood, and here is a fire-drill; having rekindled the fire, you should tend it.’”
"What if I were to produce fire and attend to that fire?
Then, dear son, I split a fire-drill with an axe, thinking:
"Perhaps I might obtain fire."
I did not find fire.
I split the fire-drill wood into two, I split it into three, I split it into four, I split it into five, I split it into ten, I split it into a hundred;
I reduced it to pieces, I reduced it to pieces.
I pounded it in a mortar; having pounded it in the mortar, I winnowed it in a strong wind, thinking, "Perhaps I might obtain fire.
Yet I did not obtain fire.
Then it occurred to that fire-worshipping matted-hair ascetic:
"How foolish and incompetent this boy is! How indeed can he seek fire in such an improper manner?
While he was watching, [the ascetic] took the fire-drill, produced a fire, and said this to the boy:
“In this way, dear son, fire should be produced;
not at all as you, being foolish, incompetent, and unmethodical, have sought fire.
“In just the same way, royal sage, you, being foolish, incompetent, and unmethodical, will seek the world beyond.”
"Relinquish this evil course of view, Prince; relinquish this evil course of view, Prince.
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
"Even though Master Kassapa speaks thus, I am still unable to relinquish this evil course of view."
King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, and kings beyond his borders also know me:
"The royal seer Pāyāsi speaks thus and holds this view:
'In this way, there is no other world; there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.'"
"If I were to relinquish this evil speculative view, Master Kassapa, there would be those who would say of me:
'The prince Pāyāsi is as foolish, incompetent, and a holder of false views as he is.
Out of anger I shall take it away; out of hypocrisy I shall take it away; out of fear I shall take it away."
2.11. The Simile of the Two Caravans:
“In that case, royal sage, I shall give you a simile.
For by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said.”
Once upon a time, royal prince, a great caravan of a thousand carts set out from the eastern country toward the western country.
Wherever it went, it quickly exhausted the grass, wood, water, green leaves, and foliage.
Now, in that caravan there were two caravan leaders: one for five hundred carts and one for five hundred carts.
Then it occurred to those caravan leaders:
“This great caravan of carts consists of a thousand vehicles;
wherever we go, our grass, wood, water, and green leaves are quickly exhausted.”
"What if we were to divide this caravan into two groups—five hundred carts on one side and five hundred carts on the other?
They divided the caravan into two groups: five hundred carts on one side and five hundred carts on the other.
A certain caravan leader, having loaded much grass, wood, and water, set out with his caravan.
After traveling for two or three days, that caravan saw a man coming toward them from the opposite direction in a fine chariot;
he was dark-skinned with red eyes, equipped with a quiver, wearing a garland of white water-lilies, dressed in wet clothes, and with wet hair, while his wheels were splattered with mud.
Seeing him approaching, he said this:
"From where, sir, are you coming?
"From such-and-such a country."
“Where are you going?
“To such-and-such a country.
“I hope, sir, that a great rain has fallen upon the wilderness ahead?”
“‘Yes, sir; thus a great cloud has rained down upon the wilderness ahead, the roads are drenched with water, and there is abundant grass, wood, and water.
Discard, sirs, your old grass, wood, and water; go as quickly as possible with your carts lightened by their loads, lest you exhaust your draft animals.
Then that caravan leader addressed the carters:”
“Sirs, this man says:
‘A great cloud has rained down upon the desert ahead; the roads are drenched with water, and there is plenty of grass, wood, and water.
Sirs, discard your old grass, wood, and water; go as quickly as possible with lightened carts, lest you exhaust your draft animals.’”
"Discard, sirs, the old grass, wood, and water; set the caravan in motion with lightly loaded carts.
"Very well, sir," those merchants replied to the caravan leader, and having discarded the old grass, wood, and water, they set the caravan in motion with lightly loaded carts.
Yet at the first caravan encampment, they did not find any grass, wood, or water.
A second time at the caravan rest-house… a third time at the caravan rest-house… a fourth time at the caravan rest-house…
In the fifth caravan encampment...
in the sixth caravan encampment...
and in the seventh caravan encampment, they did not see even grass, wood, or water.
Everyone met with misfortune and ruin.
Whether they were human beings or animals in that caravan, that non-human yakkha devoured them all;
nothing remained but bones.
When the second caravan leader realized, “Sirs,
that caravan has now traveled far,” he loaded much grass, wood, and water and set the caravan in motion.
After traveling for two or three days, that caravan saw a man who was dark-skinned with red eyes, wearing a quiver.
Seeing Kumudamālī coming toward him in a fine chariot with wheels smeared with mud, his clothes wet and his hair wet,
he said this: “From where, sir, are you coming?”
‘From such-and-such a country.
‘Where will you go?
‘To such-and-such a country.’
“Has a great rain cloud poured down upon the desert ahead, sir?
“Yes, sir, a great rain cloud has poured down upon the desert ahead. The roads are flooded with water; there is plenty of grass, wood, and water.
Discard, sir, your old grass, wood, and water; go as quickly as possible with light-laden carts, lest your draft animals become exhausted.”
Then that caravan leader addressed the merchants:
"Gentlemen, this man says:
'In the wilderness ahead, a great cloud has rained down; the roads are saturated with water, and there is much grass, wood, and water.'"
"Discard, sirs, the old grass, wood, and water; proceed as quickly as possible with lightened carts; do not weary the draft animals.
"This man, sirs, is neither our friend nor a relative by blood; why should we travel on his word?
You must not discard the old grass, wood, and water; proceed with the caravan with the goods you have already brought."
"We will not discard our old [provisions]," they said.
"Very well, sir," those caravan leaders replied to the merchant leader, and they set out with the goods as they had been loaded.
Yet, at the first caravan station, they did not see even a blade of grass, a piece of wood, or water.
At the second caravan encampment… at the third caravan encampment… at the fourth caravan encampment…
On the fifth caravan encampment… on the sixth caravan encampment… and on the seventh caravan encampment,
they did not see even a blade of grass, a piece of wood, or water.
And they saw that caravan had met with misfortune and disaster.
They saw only the bones of those who were in that caravan—whether humans or animals—who had been devoured by that non-human *yakkha*.
Then the caravan leader addressed the merchants:
“Sirs, this caravan has indeed met with disaster and ruin because of that foolish caravan leader.
Therefore, sirs, discard whatever goods of small value are in our own caravan and take whatever goods of great value are in this [other] caravan.
“Very well, sir,” those merchants replied to that caravan leader, and they [discarded] whatever [goods] were in their own caravan...
"Discarding those goods that were of little value and taking up those goods in that caravan that were of great value,
they crossed that wilderness in safety, just as was done by the wise caravan leader who acted as their guide.
In the very same way, Prince, you— a fool and incompetent— will meet with misfortune and ruin while seeking the next world in an improper manner, just like that former caravan leader."
"Those who think that you should be listened to and believed will also meet with calamity and disaster, just like those caravan leaders.
Relinquish this evil view, Prince; relinquish this evil view, Prince.
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time."
“Even though Master Kassapa speaks thus, I am still unable to relinquish this evil speculative view.
King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, as do kings abroad, as one who holds such a doctrine and such a view:
‘There is indeed no other world... [as before] ...no result of deeds.’”
"If I were to relinquish this evil view, Master Kassapa, people would say of me:
'How foolish Prince Pāyāsi is! He is incompetent and holds a mistaken grasp.
Out of anger I will carry it away; out of hypocrisy I will carry it away; out of fear I will carry it away."
2.12. The Simile of the Dung-Carrier:
"Therefore, royal sage, I shall give you a simile.
For by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said."
Once upon a time, royal prince, a certain man who raised pigs went from his own village to another village.
There he saw a large quantity of dry dung that had been discarded.
Having seen it, this thought occurred to him:
“This is indeed a large amount of dried dung that has been discarded, and it is food for my pigs.
What if I were to carry this dried dung away from here?
He spread out his upper robe, scattered the large amount of dried dung upon it, tied it into a bundle, hoisted it onto his head, and departed.
On his way, a great unseasonable cloud rained down.
Dripping and trickling, he went along smeared with excrement up to his fingernails, carrying a load of dung.
When people saw him, they said this:
“Are you not mad, my man? Are you not out of your mind? For how can you carry a load of dung, smeared with dung up to your fingernails, while it is dripping and trickling?
“It is you who are mad here, my man; it is you who are out of your mind, for this is my pig’s feed!
“In the same way, Prince, you seem to me to be like a carrier of dung.”
“Relinquish this evil view, Prince; relinquish this evil view, Prince.
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
“Even though Master Kassapa says this, I still cannot relinquish this evil view.”
King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, and other kings also know:
"The royal seer Pāyāsi speaks thus and holds this view:
'In this way, there is no other world... [and so on] ...no result of kamma.'"
“If, Master Kassapa, I were to relinquish this evil speculative view, people would say of me:
‘The prince Pāyāsi is so foolish, incompetent, and a holder of wrong grasp.
Out of anger I will take it away; out of hypocrisy I will take it away; out of fear I will take it away.”
2.13. The Simile of the Dice-Player:
“In that case, royal sage, I shall give you a simile;
for by means of a simile some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said.”
Once upon a time, royal sage, two dice-players were playing with dice.
One of the dice-players swallowed every loss as it came.
The second dice-player saw that first dice-player swallowing every loss as it came; having seen this, he said this to that dice-player:
“You are certainly winning, my friend; give me back my dice, my friend, and I shall play.
“Very well, my friend,” he replied, and that gambler gave the dice to the other gambler.
Then that gambler, having steeped the dice in poison, said this to the other gambler:
“Come, friend, let us play with dice.
“Very well, friend,” that dice-player replied to the other dice-player.
And for a second time, those dice-players played with dice.
A second time, that dice-player swallowed each loss as it came.
Then the second dice-player saw that dice-player swallowing each loss as it came for a second time; having seen him, he said this to that dice-player:
"Smeared with the highest brilliance..."
“A man does not realize he is swallowing poison:
‘Swallow it, swallow it, you wicked gambler!
Later it will turn bitter for you.’”
"In the same way, royal sage, you seem to me to be like a gambler at dice.
Abandon this evil course of view, royal sage; abandon this evil course of view, royal sage!
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time."
“Even though Master Kassapa speaks thus, I am nevertheless unable to relinquish this evil speculative view.
King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, as do kings abroad:
‘The royal prince Pāyāsi holds such a doctrine and such a view:’”
‘Thus there is no other world... nor is there any result of deeds.
If I were to relinquish this evil view, Master Kassapa, people would say of me:
‘The prince Pāyāsi was so foolish, incompetent, and a holder of wrong views!’”
“I will take it away by force, I will take it away by fraud,
I will take it away by deception.
“In that case, royal sage, I shall give you a simile.”
By means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said.
Once upon a time, royal prince, a certain district was struck by a plague.
Then one friend addressed another friend:
"Come, friend, let us go to that district; perhaps we might acquire some wealth there.
"Very well, friend," the companion replied to his companion.
They approached that district, a certain village settlement, and there they saw a great quantity of hemp discarded. Having seen it, the companion addressed his companion:
“Friend, there is indeed a great deal of discarded hemp here. Come then, friend, you bind a bundle of hemp and I shall bind a bundle of hemp; we will both take our bundles of hemp and go.
“Very well, friend,” the companion replied to his companion, and having bound a bundle of hemp, they both took their bundles of hemp and approached a certain village settlement.
There they saw a great deal of discarded hemp yarn, and seeing it, the companion addressed his companion:
“Friend, for whatever purpose we might desire linen, here is this abundant linen thread that has been discarded.
Come then, friend, you discard your load of hemp and I shall discard mine; let us both go, taking up our loads of linen thread.
“Friend, this load of hemp of mine has been carried from afar and is well-fastened; it is enough for me. You understand.”
Then that companion, having discarded his load of hemp, took up a load of hemp-thread.
They approached a certain village settlement.
There they saw many pieces of hemp discarded; seeing them, the companion addressed his companion:
“Friend, for whatever purpose we might desire hemp or hemp-thread, these abundant hemp-cloths have been discarded.
Come then, friend, you discard your load of hemp and I shall discard my load of hemp-thread; let us both go taking our loads of hemp-cloth.
“But this load of hemp, friend, has been carried from afar and is well-secured; it is enough for me, you understand.”
Then that companion, having discarded his bundle of hemp-thread, took up a bundle of hempen cloth.
They approached a certain village settlement.
There they saw a large quantity of discarded linen cloth; having seen it... [and so on].
Having seen a large quantity of discarded linen thread...
having seen a large quantity of discarded linen cloth...
having seen a large quantity of discarded cotton...
Having seen a large quantity of cotton thread discarded...
having seen a large quantity of cotton cloth discarded...
having seen a large quantity of iron discarded...
Having seen a large quantity of copper discarded… having seen a large quantity of tin discarded… having seen a large quantity of lead discarded…
Seeing a large quantity of hemp discarded...
seeing a large quantity of gold discarded, one companion addressed the other:
"Friend, for whatever purpose we might desire hemp, or hemp thread, or hemp cloth, or linen..."
“Whether it be linen thread or linen cloth, cotton thread or cotton cloth, or iron, copper, tin, lead, or silver—this is a great deal of gold that has been discarded.
Therefore, my friend, you discard your load of hemp and I shall discard my load of silver; let us both take up loads of gold and go.”
“Friend, this hemp load of mine has been carried from afar and is well-secured; you may know that it is enough for me.
Then that companion cast away his load of lead and took up a load of gold.
They both proceeded toward their own village.

In that case, as for the companion who went away taking the load of hemp, neither his parents rejoiced in him, nor did his wife and children rejoice in him, nor did his friends and colleagues rejoice in him; and on account of that, he did not obtain happiness or joy.

But as for the companion who went away taking the load of gold, his parents rejoiced in him, his wife and children rejoiced in him, and his friends and colleagues also rejoiced in him; and on account of that, he obtained happiness and joy.
"In the same way, Prince, you seem to me like the hemp-carrying porter.
Abandon this evil course of view, Prince; abandon this evil course of view, Prince!
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time."
3. Going for Refuge:
“By the previous simile alone, I was already satisfied and delighted with Master Kassapa.
Nevertheless, desiring to hear these various inspired responses to questions, I thought that I should challenge Master Kassapa. [End of Discourse on Going for Refuge]”
“Excellent, Master Kassapa! Excellent, Master Kassapa!

Just as, Master Kassapa, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—[even so has this Dhamma been made clear by Master Kassapa].”
"In this very way, Master Kassapa, the Dhamma has been proclaimed by you in many ways.
Therefore, Master Kassapa, I go for refuge to that Blessed One Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Kassapa accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
“Master Kassapa, I wish to perform a great sacrifice. May Master Kassapa instruct me in that which will be for my benefit and happiness for a long time.
“Prince, in a sacrifice of such a kind where cattle are slaughtered, or goats and sheep are slaughtered, or chickens and pigs... [are slaughtered]...”
Or they are slaughtered, or various living beings meet their destruction;
and those who receive the offerings hold wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
Such a sacrifice, O Rājakanna, yields no great fruit, no great benefit, no great splendor, and no great radiance.
"Suppose, royal sage, a farmer were to take seed and a plough and enter a forest.

There, in a field that is poor soil, with bad ground, where stumps and thorns have not been cleared away, he would plant seeds that are broken, rotten, damaged by wind and sun, lacking in essence, and poorly sown.
And the rain-god did not send down a timely and proper shower."
“Would those seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance, or would the farmer obtain a bountiful harvest?
“No indeed, Master Kassapa.
“In the same way, royal prince, in a sacrifice such as this where cattle are slaughtered, or goats and sheep are slaughtered, or chickens and pigs...”
Or [animals] are slaughtered, or various living beings meet their destruction; and the recipients are possessed of wrong view,
wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—
such a sacrifice, O Rājakanna, yields no great fruit, no great benefit, no great splendor, and no great result.
But when, O royal sage, in a sacrifice neither cows are slain, nor goats and sheep are slain, nor fowl and pigs are slain,
nor various living beings are subjected to slaughter, and the recipients possess right view,
right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—
"Indeed, royal sage, such a sacrifice is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance.
It is just as if, royal sage, a farmer were to take seed and a plow and enter a forest.

There, in a fertile field on good ground where stumps and thorns have been well cleared away, he would plant seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind or heat, substantial, and well-sown."
“And if one were to provide them with water properly from time to time,
would those seeds reach growth, increase, and abundance, and would the farmer obtain a bountiful harvest?
“Yes, Master Kassapa.”
“In the same way, royal sage, in a sacrifice of such a kind where neither cattle are slain, nor goats and sheep are slain, nor fowl and pigs are slain,
nor various living beings are brought to destruction, and where there are recipients who possess right view,
right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness— ”
“Right concentration— such a sacrifice, Prince, is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance.
Then the Prince Pāyāsi established a gift for ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, and beggars.
In that gift, such food was given: broken rice with sour gruel as the second course, and coarse garments with tassels of jaggery.
In that gift, a young brahmin named Uttara was occupied;
having given the gift, he dedicated it in this way:
“By this gift, may I meet only with Prince Pāyāsi in this world, and not in the next.
Prince Pāyāsi heard:
“The young brahmin Uttara, it seems, after giving a gift, makes this dedication:”
“By this gift, may I meet only with Prince Pāyāsi in this world, and not in the next.
Then Prince Pāyāsi summoned the young brahmin Uttara and said to him:
“Is it true, dear Uttara, that after giving a gift, you made such a declaration?”
“By this gift, may I meet only with Prince Pāyāsi in this world, and not in the next?
“Yes, sir.
“But why, dear Uttara, having given a gift, do you direct it in such a way?”
“‘By this gift, may I meet with Prince Pāyāsi himself in this very world, and not in the next’—is that not so?
For we, dear Uttara, are seekers of merit and expect the fruit of giving itself.
“In your lordship’s giving, such food as this is distributed—boiled rice with broken grains and sour gruel—which even you, sir, [cannot eat].”
One would not wish even to touch them, much less eat from them—those heavy garments with fringes of jaggery which you would not wish even to touch with your feet, much less wear.
Yet you are dear and pleasing to us; how can we unite what is pleasing with what is displeasing?”
“In that case, dear Uttara, prepare the same kind of food that I eat,
and prepare the same kind of clothes that I wear. “Very well,
sir,” the young brahmin Uttara replied to Prince Pāyāsi, and he prepared the same kind of food that Prince Pāyāsi ate.
And whatever kinds of garments Prince Pāyāsi wore, he had those same kinds of garments set out [as offerings].
Then, having given gifts without respect, having given gifts not with his own hand,
having given gifts without a devoted mind, and having given gifts that were discarded, Prince Pāyāsi, with the breakup of the body, after death, [was reborn] among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
He was reborn in companionship with him in the empty Serīsaka mansion.
As for the young brahmin named Uttara, who had been occupied with his almsgiving— he, having given a gift with due care,
having given the gift with his own hand, having given the gift with reverence, and having given the gift without casting it away, at the breaking up of the body, after death—
He was reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
At that time, the Venerable Gavampati would frequently go to the empty Serīsaka Mansion for his midday rest.
Then the deva-son Pāyāsi approached the Venerable Gavampati;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Gavampati, he stood to one side. As the deva-son Pāyāsi was standing to one side, the Venerable Gavampati said this to him:
“Who are you, friend?
“I am Pāyāsi, the royal prince, venerable sir.
“Did you not hold such a view as this, friend:”
‘In this way there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds’?
“Truly, Bhante, I held such a view:
‘In this way there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds.’”
“Moreover, I have been separated from this evil state of views by the noble Kumāra Kassapa.
“But as for that young brahmin named Uttara who was occupied with your giving, friend, where has he been reborn?
“Venerable sir, that young brahmin named Uttara who was occupied with my giving, having given that gift respectfully with his own hands...”
Having given a gift with respect, having given a gift with honor, and having given a gift that was not discarded, after the breakup of the body, after death,
he was reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
But I, venerable sir, having given a gift without respect, having given a gift not with my own hand, and having given a gift without honor—
Having given a gift that was subsequently discarded, and having given a gift, at the breaking up of the body after death,
he was reborn in the company of the Cātumahārājika devas in the empty Serīsaka mansion.
Therefore, venerable Gavampati, go to the human world and announce this:
“Give gifts respectfully; give gifts with your own hands; give gifts with a sense of reverence; give gifts that are not discarded.

After giving gifts disrespectfully, giving gifts without his own hands, giving gifts without a sense of reverence, and giving gifts that were discarded, Prince Pāyāsi, with the breakup of the body, after death, [was reborn] in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings.”
He was reborn in the empty Serīsaka mansion.
As for the young brahmin named Uttara who had been occupied with his giving— having given gifts respectfully, having given gifts with his own hands,
having given gifts with due honor, and having given gifts that were not discarded— he, upon the breakup of the body after death, [was reborn in a good destination].
“...he has been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Then the Venerable Gavampati, having returned to the human world, proclaimed:
“Give gifts with care; give gifts with your own hands; give gifts respectfully; give gifts that are not discarded.”
Having given gifts without respect, having given gifts not with his own hand, having given gifts without due honor,

and having given gifts that were discarded, the royal chaplain Pāyāsi, upon the breakup of the body after death, was reborn in companionship with the gods of the Four Great Kings in the empty Serīsaka mansion.
But the young brahmin named Uttara, who was occupied with that giving— having given gifts respectfully, having given gifts with his own hands, having given gifts with due honor,
and having given gifts not cast aside— upon the dissolution of the body, after death,
was reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
The Pāyāsi Sutta, the tenth, is finished.
The Mahāvagga is finished. Its summary verse (uddāna) is as follows:
The Nidāna of the Great Discourse,
the beautiful Nibbāna,
Janavasabha, and Govinda.
The *Samaya*, the *Sakkapañha*,
and the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna*;
the *Pāyāsi* would be the tenth.
The Mahāvagga Pāḷi is concluded.
